title: How do you count snow leopards you can hardly ever see?
blurb: Snow leopards hide among the rocks of Ladakh. Scientists from the Wildlife Institute of India used nearly a thousand hidden cameras, and told each cat apart by the spots on their forehead.

cover.alt: A snow leopard with thick spotted fur, photographed close up by a hidden camera on a rocky, snowy slope in Ladakh.
cover.credit: Figure 2G, Raina et al., PLOS ONE 2025, CC BY 4.0

original.title: Comprehensive assessment of snow leopard distribution and population in the Indian Trans-Himalaya, Ladakh: Standardizing methods for evidence-based conservation
original.authors: Raina, P., Mungi, N. A., Kumar, U., Rathi, A. D., Khan, N. H., and others, with Jhala, Y. V.

cards.b: Snow leopards live high in cold, rocky mountains. Their grey spotted fur hides them so well that people call them ghosts of the mountains. To protect them, we need to know how many there are and where they live. But how do you count a big cat you almost never see?

Pankaj Raina, Ninad Mungi, Ujjwal Kumar, Bivash Pandav and Yadvendradev Jhala are among the scientists from the Wildlife Institute of India in Dehradun. They worked with the Department of Wildlife Protection of Ladakh, including Jigmet Takpa, and with Lex Hiby from Cambridge, England, who makes software that matches patterns. They published in 2025.

First, teams walked over 6,000 kilometres of mountain paths, looking for snow leopard droppings, scrapes and pug marks, which are paw prints. Then they set up 956 hidden cameras that click when an animal walks past. A smell lure made the cats stop and bend their heads, so the camera saw the forehead. Lex Hiby's computer program then matched the spot pattern on each forehead.

img.alt: A snow leopard's face on a computer screen, with a green grid fitted over the forehead so the spots can be matched.
img.credit: Figure 2B, Raina et al., PLOS ONE 2025, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: The cameras took over 26,000 photos of snow leopards. From their foreheads, the team told apart 126 different cats. From this, they worked out that about 477 snow leopards live in Ladakh. That is one of the biggest groups in the world. Most lived where there were plenty of wild sheep and goats, like bharal and ibex, to hunt.

img.alt: A black and white night photo from a hidden camera, showing a snow leopard walking straight towards the camera with glowing eyes.
img.credit: Figure 2H, Raina et al., PLOS ONE 2025, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: The cameras could not cover every corner, so 477 is a careful estimate. The real number is probably between about 380 and 600. Using the forehead instead of the side of the body helped. Body fur is long and blows in the wind, but forehead spots stay the same. Older cameras sometimes took blurry photos.

Most of these snow leopards live in places shared with herders and their animals, not in parks. Sometimes snow leopards kill sheep and goats, and people get angry. Knowing where the cats live helps plan new roads and towns, and helps people and snow leopards share the mountains. India now has a photo library of every cat found.

Tell animals apart by their marks, as the snow leopard team did with foreheads. For a week, watch the crows, pigeons or street dogs near your home. Draw or photograph any mark that makes one different, like a white patch or a torn feather. Can you recognise the same animal on another day? How many different ones have you met?

Snow leopards sometimes kill a family's sheep, and that family may lose money. Should the family be paid back? Or should herders guard their animals better at night? Who should share the cost of living near wild animals: the herders, the government, or all of us?
